result: Motor units in WT and SOD1G93A mice were classified into FF, FR, and S types based on contractile properties (twitch amplitude, contraction time, fatigue index). The classification used cutoff values of 20 ms for contraction time and 8 mN for twitch force. The proportions of motor unit types were similar between WT and SOD1G93A mice.
evaluation: Claims C27-C37 provide comprehensive methodological details and quantitative data for motor unit classification. The classification scheme is well-justified by the data shown in Figures 1-2, with clear cutoff values and statistical validation (χ² test p=0.28). The inter-relationships between contractile properties support the validity of the classification approach.

result: In SOD1G93A mice, motoneurons innervating FF and large FR motor units (>1.3 mN) lose the ability to fire repetitively before denervation of neuromuscular junctions. This hypoexcitability was significantly more frequent in SOD1G93A (21%) than WT (6%) mice, with 40% of FF units and 46% of large FR units affected, while all small FR and S units retained repetitive firing.
evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C40-C50, C64 collectively demonstrate selective hypoexcitability in vulnerable motor units with strong statistical support (Fisher exact test p=0.01, ANOVA p<0.001). The data clearly show that loss of repetitive firing occurs before denervation (C42) and is selective for large motor units (C44-C49), supported by Figures 3D-F.

result: Non-repetitively firing motoneurons had larger input conductances and more depolarized resting membrane potentials than repetitively firing motoneurons. In SOD1G93A mice, non-firing motoneurons rested at −62±8 mV versus −68±8 mV for firing motoneurons, and the largest motor units were more depolarized in mutants than controls.
evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 for input conductance, p=0.01 for membrane potential) and data in Figure 3G-H and Table 2. The findings are internally consistent and link electrophysiological properties to firing capability.

result: Motoneurons that retained repetitive firing capability showed normal excitability in SOD1G93A mice. Recruitment current, voltage excursion, and gain were unchanged compared to WT mice, with the slope of the recruitment current-input conductance relationship unaffected (ANCOVA p=0.99).
evaluation: Claims C57-C63, C65 demonstrate preserved excitability in firing motoneurons with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney, ANCOVA) and data in Figure 4 and Table 2. The linear relationship between recruitment current and input conductance (r²=0.81, p<0.0001) supports the validity of the measurements.

result: In the FUS-ALS model (τONFUSP525L mice), large motor units showed progressive hypoexcitability similar to SOD1G93A mice. At P180 in ankle flexors, 68% of large motor units (>1.3 mN) in FUSP525L mice were non-firing versus 18% in controls (p=0.003), while small motor units were unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C20, C66-C78 demonstrate that hypoexcitability is not specific to SOD1 mutations, supported by statistical analyses (Fisher exact tests) and data in Figure 5. The temporal and motor pool-specific patterns strengthen the generalizability of the findings, though the sample sizes for some comparisons are modest.

result: In FUSP525L mice at P180, non-firing ankle flexor motoneurons had more depolarized resting potentials than firing motoneurons (two-way ANOVA p=0.001), while firing motoneurons retained normal excitability with unchanged recruitment current and input conductance relationship (ANCOVA p=0.19).
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by statistical analyses and data in Figure 6, confirming that the pattern observed in SOD1G93A mice generalizes to the FUS model. The consistency across models strengthens the overall conclusions.

result: Chodl expression in WT mice was selective for FF motoneurons and large FR motoneurons (>1.3 mN), with 8/9 large motor units expressing Chodl versus 2/10 small motor units. Chodl+ motor units developed significantly more force (8.1±8.6 mN) than Chodl− units (0.8±0.6 mN, p<0.0001), indicating FR motoneurons comprise two distinct subpopulations.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C83-C88 combine electrophysiology with molecular markers to demonstrate FR heterogeneity. The data in Figure 7 show clear separation between Chodl+ and Chodl− populations with strong statistical support. However, the sample size is modest (N=19 motoneurons), and the correlation with hypoexcitability pattern is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

result: Disease marker analysis showed that non-firing motoneurons had lower p-eIF2α levels (0.2±0.2) than firing motoneurons (0.8±0.2, p=0.02), while p62 aggregates were variable but high in some non-firing cells. This pattern suggests non-firing motoneurons are at a more advanced disease stage than firing motoneurons.
evaluation: Claims C89-C103 provide important mechanistic insights, but the sample size is very small (N=8 motoneurons total, 4 firing and 4 non-firing from 6 mice). The p-eIF2α finding is statistically significant but based on minimal replication. The p62 data are more variable and less conclusive (C101-C102). While the interpretation is plausible given prior literature (C92), the limited sample size and variability in p62 expression warrant caution.

result: The study concludes that intrinsic hyperexcitability is unlikely to cause motoneuron degeneration in ALS. Instead, hypoexcitability (loss of repetitive firing) precedes denervation and represents an early sign of degeneration, with this mechanism generalizing across two unrelated ALS models.
evaluation: Claims C3, C26, C105, C126 represent the main conclusions, well-supported by the convergent evidence from SOD1G93A and FUSP525L models (C2, C19, C20, C42, C64). The demonstration that hypoexcitability occurs before denervation in vulnerable motor units across two models provides strong support for this conclusion.

result: Prior literature shows conflicting evidence on motoneuron excitability in ALS models, with hyperexcitability reported in embryonic and some neonatal stages, but hypoexcitability emerging in adults. The most vulnerable motoneurons (FF type) are the first to degenerate, followed by FR, with S-type being most resistant.
evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C18 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the context and rationale for the current study, highlighting the controversy about excitability changes and the selective vulnerability of motor unit types.

result: FF motor units in SOD1G93A mice displayed slightly longer contraction times than in WT mice, which might reflect desynchronization of muscle fibers preceding denervation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by data in Table 1 showing statistically significant differences (p=0.005). However, C39 is speculative about the mechanism. The observation is valid but the interpretation requires further validation.

result: This is the first study in a mouse model of ALS to correlate changes in electrical properties of motoneurons with the physiological type of their motor unit.
evaluation: Claim C104 is a statement about the novelty of the approach. The methodology combining in vivo intracellular recording with motor unit characterization in non-paralyzed mice is indeed novel for ALS models, as supported by the methodological descriptions and citations.

result: Loss of repetitive firing develops progressively during ALS, with 35% of motoneurons affected by P30-P60. This loss is unrelated to anesthesia and parallels findings in iPSC-derived motoneurons from ALS patients, which transition from hyperexcitable to hypoexcitable over time.
evaluation: Claims C106-C112 integrate current findings with prior work (citations to Delestrée et al., 2014 and iPSC studies). The consistency across mouse models and human iPSC-derived neurons strengthens the translational relevance, though these are primarily literature-based claims.

result: Mechanistic hypotheses suggest that loss of repetitive firing may result from insufficient persistent sodium current, imbalance in sodium/potassium currents, or membrane depolarization due to reduced ATP availability. Theoretical modeling suggests membrane depolarization is greatest at distal axon and decreasing firing rate may be compensatory to prevent energy crisis.
evaluation: Claims C113-C120 present mechanistic hypotheses based on literature (citations to Delestrée, Huh, Sareen, Devlin, Naujock, Le Masson studies). While these are plausible mechanisms consistent with the observations, they are not directly tested in this study. The claims appropriately use speculative language (C113, C120) but represent inferences rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

result: Pharmacological and chemogenetic studies suggest that modulating excitability has therapeutic potential: early enhancement of excitability or late reduction of hypoexcitability may be beneficial, supporting a model where hypoexcitability contributes to motoneuron degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C121-C125 summarize prior therapeutic studies (Wainger, Naujock, Saxena) that support the functional significance of excitability changes. These literature-based claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings, though they do not represent new data from this study.
